opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it makes for a great press release. You've got a company, say Volkswagen or whoever, and they can say "we're using a quantum computer to optimize our bus routes," and that sounds incredibly futuristic. It gets headlines, it signals that they're on the cutting edge, and D-Wave is of course very happy to have that partnership. Everybody gets something out of it from a marketing standpoint.

But if you ask the scientific question, which is the only one I really care about: is the quantum computer actually doing anything there that you couldn't do as well or better with a classical computer? As far as I've ever been able to tell, the answer has been no. Vehicle routing is a classic optimization problem, and there are extremely good classical heuristics for it: simulated annealing, tabu search, integer programming solvers like Gurobi that people have spent decades tuning. When researchers have done careful head-to-head comparisons between D-Wave's devices and the best classical algorithms, rather than straw-man classical algorithms, the quantum advantage has either vanished or never been convincingly shown to exist.

And there's a deeper theoretical point. These are NP-hard optimization problems, and we have no reason to believe that quantum computers, let alone quantum annealers with noisy qubits and limited connectivity, can solve NP-hard problems efficiently in general. The best you could hope for is maybe some modest speedup on certain instances, and even that hasn't been clearly demonstrated for annealing. Often a lot of the actual work in these demos is being done by classical preprocessing and postprocessing, and the quantum part is a small piece of the pipeline.

So I've spent, what, well over a decade now as sort of the "Chief D-Wave Skeptic," and my position hasn't been that quantum computing is fake. I think quantum computing is one of the most exciting things in science. Things like Shor's algorithm or simulating quantum chemistry have real, theoretically grounded reasons for an exponential speedup. My position has been that you need to separate the real science from the hype. When a company advertises quantum vehicle routing, the question to ask is: compared to what? Did you benchmark against the best classical method? Usually that question doesn't get a satisfying answer.

r001.rationale: The response says the company gets headlines and signals it is cutting edge, while D-Wave benefits from the partnership, giving both publicity value.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, I think the honest answer is that it's marketing. It's not that the companies are lying, exactly — I'm sure Volkswagen or whoever really did run some optimization problem on a D-Wave machine. The question is whether the quantum computer was actually doing anything that you couldn't have done just as well, or better, or a thousand times faster, on a laptop running a classical algorithm. And in every case I've looked at, the answer has been no.

What D-Wave builds is a quantum annealer. It's a special-purpose device for optimization, and the hope was always that quantum tunneling would let it escape local minima that a classical annealer would get stuck in. That's a perfectly respectable hypothesis. But when people have actually done careful comparisons against classical algorithms — not against some naive algorithm, but against the best thing a competent person would write — the quantum speedup has mostly evaporated. There's a long history here: every few years there's an announcement of a 100-million-fold speedup, and then Matthias Troyer or Umesh Vazirani or someone points out that if you just use simulated annealing properly, or a better classical heuristic, the advantage disappears.

So why do companies do it? I think there are a few reasons. One is that quantum computing sounds futuristic, and an announcement that says "we're using a quantum computer to route our buses" gets you press coverage that "we tuned our linear programming solver" never will. Another is that there's genuine curiosity — companies want to get their hands on this technology early so they're not caught flat-footed if it ever does become useful, and I actually think that's defensible as long as everyone's honest about what's going on. And the third is that D-Wave itself has been very good at making partnerships that generate headlines.

My complaint has never been with the engineering — D-Wave built a real, interesting machine. My complaint is with the framing. When a press release implies that a quantum computer has solved a real-world logistics problem in a way classical computers can't, that's just not true today, and I think it ultimately hurts the field, because when people later realize it, they conclude the whole thing was hype. The actual case for quantum computing is strong enough that it doesn't need these inflated claims. The real speedups we know about — Shor's algorithm, quantum simulation — those are for very specific problems, and vehicle routing isn't one of them.

r001.rationale: The response says companies gain press coverage by announcing quantum vehicle routing and that D-Wave partnerships generate headlines, communicating publicity benefits for both.

astra-6.text:
Well, there’s an obvious publicity benefit. If you say, “We’re optimizing vehicle routes using a quantum computer,” that gets attention in a way that “We’re using a classical optimization algorithm” probably doesn’t.

Now, vehicle routing is a real optimization problem, and you can encode versions of it into the kind of problem that D-Wave’s machines are designed to tackle. But being able to run a problem on a quantum device is very different from showing that the device solves it faster or better than the best classical methods. That comparison is the crucial thing.

So I’d ask: What part of the computation actually happened on the D-Wave machine? What classical algorithms did they compare it against? And was there a demonstrated advantage? Without that, it might be an interesting experiment, but the advertising is getting ahead of the evidence.

r001.rationale: The response says quantum-computing claims attract attention, which conveys publicity for the routing company, but it does not explain that D-Wave also benefits from that publicity.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, vehicle routing is a genuinely important optimization problem, and it’s the kind of thing you can try to encode into the form that D-Wave’s machines accept. But there’s a big difference between running a problem on a quantum computer and showing that the quantum computer gives you an advantage over the best classical methods.

So why advertise it? There’s an obvious publicity benefit to saying you’re using a quantum computer. You might also want your people to gain experience with the technology. Those are understandable motivations. But the scientific question is: did it find better routes, faster or more cheaply, than you could have found with a classical computer? Without a convincing comparison, the announcement doesn’t tell us very much about quantum computing’s usefulness.

r001.rationale: The response says that using a quantum computer offers publicity, but it does not explain that the publicity benefits both D-Wave and the routing company.
